title: AHA/ASA Scientific Statement 2021: Primary Care of Adult Patients After Stroke

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: For anterior-circulation stroke, obtain carotid-artery imaging.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Screen for atrial fibrillation with an ECG.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Confirm the stroke diagnosis using CT or MRI of the brain.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Obtain a complete blood count, PT/INR, PTT, glucose, hemoglobin A1c, creatinine and lipid profile to characterize risk factors and inform treatment.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Help patients adopt regular physical activity, weight management and smoking cessation; avoid passive smoke, excessive alcohol, stimulants and intravenous opioids.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: For most patients with hypertension after stroke, aim for blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Use atorvastatin 80 mg daily when LDL-C exceeds 100 mg/dL and there is no major cardiac embolic source or other statin indication. The table footnote describes high-intensity statin therapy for most stroke/TIA patients, with at least 50% LDL-C lowering and, in high-risk patients including aortic-arch atheroma, LDL-C below 70 mg/dL. These are the 2021 source targets; use the 2026 dyslipidemia guideline for current risk-specific targets.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: For most patients with diabetes, target hemoglobin A1c of 7% or lower, individualized to the patient.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: For diabetes, select glucose-lowering agents with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit in addition to metformin.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Combine lifestyle measures, nutrition counseling, self-management support and medication to improve glycemia and vascular risk in diabetes.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Support weight management for patients with overweight or obesity.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: For stroke attributable to 50%–99% intracranial arterial stenosis, prescribe aspirin 325 mg daily.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Refer patients with 70%–99% ipsilateral extracranial carotid stenosis and an index event within the preceding 6 months for endarterectomy assessment. The source narrative favors treatment within 2 weeks for most eligible patients; the 6-month eligibility window is not a reason to delay surgery.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Refer appropriately selected patients with 50%–69% ipsilateral extracranial carotid stenosis for endarterectomy assessment.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Provide intensive medical therapy whether or not carotid surgery is performed: antiplatelet treatment, blood-pressure control and lipid lowering.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Use oral anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation or flutter unless contraindicated.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Prefer apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban to warfarin for atrial fibrillation/flutter, except with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Use warfarin rather than a direct oral anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation associated with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Support changes that improve stroke knowledge, lifestyle and adherence to medication.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: Address health literacy, language needs, medication affordability, food and housing insecurity, transportation and other social factors that impede risk-factor treatment.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: For noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, options include aspirin 50–325 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, or aspirin 25 mg plus extended-release dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily.

recommendations.classNote: Class I as summarized in the 2021 statement; no individual Level of Evidence is supplied in this table.
recommendations.text: After recent noncardioembolic minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4), start aspirin plus clopidogrel early, ideally within 12–24 hours, then return to one antiplatelet. The 2021 narrative restricts candidates to patients not eligible for thrombolysis, EVT, endarterectomy or anticoagulation. The table gives a 21–90-day course; the first-visit guidance favors stopping at 21 days for most eligible patients, with up to 90 days reasonable after ischemic stroke or TIA within 30 days related to severe major intracranial stenosis.

recommendations.text: A Mediterranean-style diet and sodium restriction are reasonable lifestyle measures after stroke.

Arrange the first primary-care visit soon after discharge, generally within 1–3 weeks.
Review hospital records and invite the patient to describe the event, their understanding, questions, fears and psychological effects.

Confirm the stroke mechanism, completion of the diagnostic workup and cause-specific treatment. Prioritize deferred carotid imaging and rhythm monitoring, and coordinate early decisions with neurology.
Identify time-sensitive carotid revascularization, antiplatelet and statin needs. For most eligible carotid-surgery patients, the source favors revascularization within 2 weeks.

Review DAPT eligibility and its intended stop date. The 2021 source excludes candidates for thrombolysis, EVT, endarterectomy or anticoagulation. For most eligible patients stop the second antiplatelet at about 21 days; ischemic stroke or TIA within 30 days associated with severe major intracranial stenosis may warrant up to 90 days.
Identify and correct circumstances that preceded the stroke, such as poor blood-pressure control or interrupted anticoagulation.
Keep a concise, updated stroke history covering prior risks, presenting symptoms, investigations, location, acute treatment, hospital course, presumed cause and rehabilitation progress.
Reassess medical and social circumstances and the patient’s goals. With consent, include caregivers to identify both patient and family needs, and use these priorities to shape care.

Assess anxiety, cognition, communication, contractures, depression, dysphagia, falls, fatigue, fractures, shoulder pain, mobility, osteoporosis, pressure injuries or other skin breakdown, seizures, spasticity, thromboembolism and urinary or bowel incontinence.
Screen for depression when treatment resources are available; manage identified depression using usual evidence-based depression care. PHQ-9 is one screening option discussed by the source.

Ask about communication support, cognition, mood, fear of falling, access to follow-up, daily activities, mobility, pain, rehabilitation, return to work, sexual function, spasticity and continence. Referral can still help in the subacute or chronic phase.

At follow-up, review stroke cause and prevention, blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, carotid disease, lipids and diabetes. Check actual medication use and tolerability, including fears about adverse effects.

Ask about financial strain, food insecurity, transport, education and access to care; connect patients with community resources and social work. Address language barriers and implicit bias within the practice.
Negotiate realistic goals with the patient, prioritize pressing needs and schedule timely follow-up for deferred issues. Tailor the plan to the patient’s circumstances and capacity after discharge.

Teach patients and caregivers about the condition, treatment, warning symptoms requiring emergency services, self-monitoring, problem solving and decisions. Coordinate nursing, pharmacy, social work, rehabilitation and specialty input as needed.
Choose the return-visit interval according to clinical condition, stability of risk factors and the chance that treatment goals will not be met.

Reassess ADLs, IADLs, communication and mobility in the office, even if evaluated before discharge. Figure 2 additionally covers balance/ataxia, cognition/memory, driving, neglect, sexuality, spasticity, swallowing, urination and visual, hearing or sensory function; it groups these assessments as Class I or IIa without assigning each a separate class.

Compare current ability with pre-stroke function and the patient’s goals. If rehabilitation potential remains, connect the patient to appropriate therapy; if potential has been reached, reassess periodically as needs can change.

Use a validated brief cognitive screen before discharge and during the first year, with later screening or case finding when indicated. The statement discusses Berg or Morse measures for falls and timed-up-and-go or 10-meter walking tests for mobility; formal neuropsychological testing is not routinely necessary.

Assess physical activity, counsel and refer to suitable community programs. If feasible for the individual, support general adult targets of 150 minutes weekly of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity; the minimum effective poststroke exercise dose was not established in this source.

Use an iterative improvement process with agreed methods, frontline staff and patient participation, and measures that track results. Consider pharmacy-supported care, self-monitoring and coordinated case management; education or behavior interventions alone did not improve outcomes in the cited transition studies.

extractionNote: Covers the full 2021 scientific statement’s care strategy, all 24 Table 4 prevention recommendations plus its Class IIa dietary footnote, and all 34 individually graded Figure 2 rehabilitation items. Figure 2 reproduces 2016 recommendations; these historical classes must be read alongside the superseding 2026 AHA/ASA rehabilitation guideline. Current lipid targets are in the 2026 dyslipidemia guideline.

coverage.scope: All individually graded recommendations in Table 4 and Figure 2, with all six care-strategy components and the first-visit, complication, unmet-need, functional-assessment and quality-improvement guidance represented.
